c1-speaker-inference.title: Speaker's Own Inference: shekilli
c1-speaker-inference.pattern: [clause] + shekilli (it seems/apparently, based on what I observe)
c1-speaker-inference.explanation: Shekilli hedges a claim as the SPEAKER's own inference from visible evidence, distinct from ekan (a fresh discovery), emish (distanced hearsay), and -mikan (wondering aloud): u charchagan shekilli (he/she seems tired [judging by how he/she looks]).
c1-speaker-inference.fact: Uzbek grammatically distinguishes at least four flavors of "apparently" that English collapses into one word -- shekilli (my own visual/contextual inference), ekan (a fact I just discovered), emish (something I heard secondhand, held at a distance), and -mikan (my own open-ended wondering) -- and mixing them up is one of the clearest tells of a non-native speaker at this level.

dialogue.en: He/she seems tired, worked all day.

c1-on-the-verge.title: On the Verge Of: -gudek
c1-on-the-verge.pattern: [verb stem] + -gudek + bo'lmoq (to be on the verge of ~ing / to such an extent that ~)
c1-on-the-verge.explanation: -gudek combined with bo'lmoq expresses being right on the edge of an action or state: yig'lagudek bo'ldi (he/she was on the verge of crying). It can also intensify a description to an extreme degree: kulgudek gap emas (it's not a laughing matter, literally "not talk to the extent of laughing").
c1-on-the-verge.fact: -gudek shares its -dek ending with the plain simile suffix (sher dek, "like a lion") and with -gandek ("as if") -- all three compare something to a reference point, but -gudek's reference point is a threshold not yet crossed, making it the only one of the three pointing at something imminent rather than already true or merely apparent.

dialogue.native: U bu xabarni eshitib nima qildi?
dialogue.en: What did he/she do upon hearing this news?

dialogue.native: Yig'lagudek bo'ldi, ammo o'zini tutib qoldi.
dialogue.en: He/she was on the verge of crying, but held himself/herself together.
